author: EmuCore - Hub
title: xemu adds a switchable JIT engine for the Xbox audio DSP
summary: A new DSP56300 backend gives xemu an alternative to interpreting every guest instruction. A shared state layer keeps the existing interpreter available and connects both engines to save-state handling.
heroAlt: Original Xbox console beside its Duke controller on a white background.

blocks.text: One audio processor, two execution paths

The Xbox MCPX audio processor includes a Motorola DSP56300 digital signal processor. xemu already had a C interpreter for that guest processor; pull request #2801 added a second backend that uses just-in-time compilation. The change concerns how DSP instructions run inside the emulator, rather than introducing a new audio format or a game-specific patch.
Translate instruction work ahead of execution

An interpreter decodes and dispatches guest instructions as they are reached. A JIT can translate a sequence into host instructions and reuse the generated code, trading compilation work for less repeated dispatch. The xemu change adds a Rust-based JIT alongside the C interpreter. Its benefit depends on how much time a title spends in DSP code and on the host CPU; the project did not claim one universal speedup.
Keep both engines behind a shared state boundary

The patch introduces a DSP operations interface and a common core-state representation. That boundary lets xemu select or switch execution engines without making the rest of the audio processor depend on one implementation. It also gives save and load code a common state to serialize, which is essential when a saved session is reopened with a different backend selected.
Preserve the interpreter as a useful reference

The C interpreter remains available, and the new setting allows the JIT path to be enabled or disabled. Keeping both paths helps developers compare behavior when investigating an audio discrepancy: the JIT can be checked against a simpler instruction-by-instruction implementation. The same refactor also fixes defects found in the existing interpreter, so the patch is not only a compiler addition.

Early discussion attached measurements from a small set of games and noted remaining edge cases, including audio loops and titles tied to frame rate. Those reports are useful leads, not a cross-game benchmark. The merged change establishes a second DSP engine and its state plumbing; repeatable tests across games, host CPUs, save-state transitions, and timing-sensitive audio are still needed to characterize its practical gains.
